title: Design a Content Delivery Network (CDN)
tagline: Serve files from a city near the user, and keep the origin calm.

statement.prompt: Design a **content delivery network** that serves images, scripts and video to users around the world with low latency, so most requests never reach the customer's own servers.
context: You are in a 45-minute interview. The interviewer gave you only the sentence above.
The customers are websites and streaming apps; their servers are the **origin**.
Think of Cloudflare, Akamai or CloudFront.
given: About **50 million** daily users, each downloading roughly **2 MB** through the CDN.
Peak traffic is several times the average.
Each customer's origin can serve about **1 Gbit/s**.
Content is mostly static: images, scripts and video segments.

expectations.title: Drive the conversation
expectations.body: Ask questions before drawing anything. State your assumptions out loud so they can be corrected early.

expectations.title: Use numbers
expectations.body: Turn the givens into requests per second, storage and bandwidth. Every later choice should point back to one of them.

expectations.title: Start simple, then evolve
expectations.body: Get a working version on the board first. Add caches, sharding and queues only when a number or a requirement asks for them.

expectations.title: Go deep on the hard parts
expectations.body: For this problem the hard parts are routing users to the nearest edge, getting a very high hit rate, and keeping content fresh without hammering the origin.

expectations.title: Name the trade-offs
expectations.body: Say what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change your mind.

expectations.title: Think about failure
expectations.body: Point out single points of failure and say what happens when a node, a cache or a whole zone goes down.

scope_out: Dynamic page personalisation at the edge
great: Explains **DNS or anycast** routing to the nearest healthy edge.
Calculates the **hit rate** needed to protect the origin.
Uses a **shield cache** and **request coalescing** for cold starts.

concepts.def: A cache server in a city or network close to users.
The customer's own server that holds the real content.
The same IP is announced from many places; routing sends each user to the nearest.
How long a cached copy may be used before it is checked or replaced.
The share of requests answered from cache without contacting the origin.
A link with an expiry and signature the edge can verify without asking anyone.

numbers: 50M users x 2 MB = **100 TB a day** = about **9 Gbit/s** average
Origin share = origin capacity / peak traffic, so you need roughly **97%+ hit rate**
Light travels about **1 ms per 100 km** in fibre, which is why distance matters

takeaways: A CDN is a **distributed cache** with a control plane; users are sent to the nearest healthy edge by **DNS or anycast**.
Compute the hit rate you need: **origin capacity / peak traffic**; then use **edge + shield** caches.
Prefer **versioned file names**; keep **purge** for emergencies.
Protect private content with **signed URLs** and survive origin failure with **stale-if-error**.

tradeoffs.gain: High hit rate, low origin load
tradeoffs.cost: Stale content until purged or versioned
Lower hit rate per edge, more cost

steps.title: What does a CDN do?
steps.prompt: Which belong in the **core** scope of a CDN?
steps.hint: Is it a cache or the source of truth?
steps.explain: A CDN is a **geographically distributed cache** with a control plane (expiry, purge, security).

notes: Core: serve from the nearest edge, fill from origin on miss, expiry and purge controls

options.text: Support static files and video segments
options.why: The main CDN workloads.

options.text: Let owners set expiry and purge stale content
options.why: Without control, mistakes stay live.

options.text: Serve cached content from a server near the user
options.why: The whole point.

options.text: Run the customer's database
options.why: A CDN fronts content; it is not a database.

options.text: Store the only copy of files forever
options.why: The origin remains the source of truth. A CDN is a cache.

options.text: Fetch from the origin on a cache miss and keep a copy
options.why: That is how a pull CDN fills itself.

steps.title: What qualities matter?
steps.prompt: Pick the qualities that shape a CDN.
steps.hint: What does the user feel? What does the origin owner pay for?
steps.explain: **Latency, availability, bandwidth, hit rate.** Content freshness is *eventual*, controlled by TTL and purge.

notes: Qualities: low latency, high availability, huge bandwidth, high hit rate, eventually consistent content

options.text: High availability: an edge failure should be invisible
options.why: Users are routed to the next nearest edge.

options.text: Very high throughput and bandwidth
options.why: Video makes this a bandwidth business.

options.text: Strong consistency: all edges show new content at the same instant
options.why: Impossible to guarantee cheaply. Use TTLs and purges.

options.text: Low latency to users worldwide (tens of milliseconds)
options.why: Distance is the enemy; edges shorten it.

options.text: High cache hit rate, so the origin stays calm
options.why: The origin is small compared to total traffic.

steps.title: How much bandwidth?
steps.prompt: **50 million** daily users each download **2 MB** through the CDN. What is the average **bandwidth in Gbit/s**? (1 byte = 8 bits.)
steps.hint: Total bytes a day, times 8, divided by seconds in a day.
steps.explain: About **10 Gbit/s on average and 30 or more at peak**. A single origin data centre cannot serve that. Spread over hundreds of edges it is easy. This number is the **business case** for a CDN.

notes: Load: about 100 TB/day, about 10 Gbit/s average, 30+ Gbit/s peak

work: 100 TB x 8 = 800 Tbit / 86,400 s = about **9.3 Gbit/s** average
Peak is several times higher: **30+ Gbit/s**

steps.title: What cache hit rate do you aim for?
steps.prompt: The origin can serve at most **1 Gbit/s**. Peak traffic is **30 Gbit/s**. What is the **minimum hit rate (%)** the CDN needs so the origin is not overloaded?
steps.hint: What fraction of traffic may reach the origin?
steps.explain: You need a hit rate of about **97%+**. This drives design choices: long TTLs, versioned file names, a **shield cache** and pre-warming for launches.

notes: Target: 97%+ edge hit rate; origin sees under 3% of traffic

work: Origin may serve 1 of 30 Gbit/s = **3.3%** of traffic
So at least **96.7%** must be answered by the edges

steps.title: How does a user find the nearest edge?
steps.prompt: A user in Chennai requests `cdn.example.com/logo.png`. How do we send them to a nearby, healthy edge?
steps.hint: Who knows where the user is?
steps.explain: **DNS-based geo/latency routing** or **anycast**. DNS TTLs must be short enough to move users away from a failing edge.

notes: Routing: DNS geo/latency routing or anycast to the nearest healthy edge

steps.followup: DNS answers are cached. What does that do to failover speed?

options.text: DNS returns the nearest healthy edge (latency or geo based), or anycast routes the IP to the nearest site
options.why: The standard answer. Health information keeps dead edges out.

options.text: Hard-code one edge IP in the app
options.why: No failover, no locality.

options.text: Pick a random edge
options.why: Random edges may be on another continent.

options.text: The origin server redirects every user manually
options.why: Defeats the point and overloads the origin.

steps.title: Trace a request
steps.prompt: Put the steps of a request for a file that is **not yet cached** in order.
steps.explain: Two cache layers, **edge** then **shield**, mean a viral file is fetched from the origin **once**, not once per city.

notes: Flow: edge -> regional shield -> origin; each layer stores the file with a TTL

items.text: DNS sends the user to the nearest edge
The edge looks in its cache and finds nothing (miss)
items.why: A cold edge or an expired file.

items.text: The edge asks the regional shield cache
items.why: Collapses many edge misses into one request.

items.text: The shield asks the origin, which returns the file
items.why: Only now does the origin do any work.

items.text: Shield and edge store the file with a TTL, and answer the user
items.why: Next user in the city gets a hit.

steps.title: Push or pull?
steps.prompt: A big show launches at 8 pm and millions will request the same new video within a minute. What do you do?
steps.hint: What is predictable, what is not?
steps.explain: **Pull for the long tail, push for the predictable hits.** Add **request coalescing** so simultaneous misses for the same file become one origin request.

notes: Fill: pull by default, pre-warm known hits, coalesce simultaneous misses

steps.pitfall: Not mentioning the first-request spike after a launch.
steps.followup: What does request coalescing do exactly?

options.text: Push every file in the catalogue to every edge
options.why: Wastes enormous storage on files nobody watches.

options.text: Use pull by default and **pre-warm** (push) the popular files to edges before the launch
options.why: Pull handles the long tail; pre-warming avoids a thundering herd of first misses.

options.text: Pull only and hope for the best
options.why: Thousands of simultaneous first misses can crush the origin.

options.text: Disable caching for new files
options.why: Makes it worse.

steps.title: Keeping content fresh
steps.prompt: A designer uploads a new logo with the same file name. Which mechanisms get users the new one without chaos?
steps.hint: Make it so you rarely need to delete anything.
steps.explain: **Versioned names first, purge for emergencies.** Purging works best through a control plane that fans out the command to all edges.

notes: Freshness: versioned file names, Cache-Control + ETag, purge API for emergencies

options.text: Restart all edge servers
options.why: Drops the cache for everything and floods the origin.

options.text: Provide a purge API that reaches every edge within seconds
options.why: For emergencies and unversioned content.

options.text: Wait for every cache TTL to run out naturally, whatever it is
options.why: A one-year TTL means a year of the old logo.

options.text: Set sensible `Cache-Control: max-age` and use `ETag` revalidation
options.why: Edges ask "changed?" and get a tiny 304 if not.

options.text: Version the file name or add a hash (`logo.9fd2.png`)
options.why: A new name is a new cache entry. Nothing to purge.

steps.title: What to evict when an edge is full?
steps.prompt: An edge has limited disk. Which policy suits it best?
steps.explain: **LRU plus admission control** (only cache a file after its second request) is a common practical design.

notes: Eviction: LRU with admission control for one-hit wonders

options.text: Random deletion
options.why: Throws away hot files as easily as cold.

options.text: LRU (or a size-aware variant), with admission rules so one-hit wonders do not push out popular files
options.why: Keeps recently useful files, protects against scans.

options.text: Delete the biggest files first
options.why: Large popular videos would never stay.

options.text: Never evict; buy infinite disk
options.why: Not realistic.

steps.title: Private content and attacks
steps.prompt: Some videos are paid. Which measures apply?
steps.hint: How does the edge know without asking home?
steps.explain: **Push the check to the edge** using signed tokens, so authorisation does not need a round trip to the origin.

notes: Security: signed expiring URLs, TLS at the edge, edge rate limiting

options.text: Make all content public and rely on obscure URLs
options.why: Unlisted is not private.

options.text: Rate limiting and DDoS absorption at the edge
options.why: A distributed network is a natural shock absorber.

options.text: TLS at the edge with certificates managed centrally
options.why: Users connect securely to the nearby edge.

options.text: Check a database on every request for permission
options.why: Adds latency and load to the hot path. Signed URLs avoid it.

options.text: **Signed URLs or cookies** that expire
options.why: The edge verifies the signature and time before serving.

steps.title: Failures
steps.hint: What can we still serve from memory?
steps.explain: Design so the **cache protects the origin and the origin does not break the cache**: stale-if-error, coalescing, timeouts and multi-region origins.

notes: Failure: reroute from dead edges, serve stale if origin errors, multi-region origin, bounded retries

options.text: Origin down: return errors immediately to protect the CDN
options.why: Hurts users when cached content could still be served.

options.text: Edge dies: DNS or anycast routes users to the next nearest edge
options.why: Hit rate dips, service continues.

options.text: Replicate the origin in two regions with health-checked failover
options.why: Removes the origin single point of failure.

options.text: Origin down: serve stale content (`stale-if-error`) while it recovers
options.why: Slightly old beats an error page.

options.text: Retry origin fetches with no limit
options.why: A retry storm on a struggling origin.

steps.title: Defend your design
steps.prompt: In two or three sentences: what does a CDN trade away to get speed?
steps.hint: Freshness, cost and number of layers.
steps.explain: Strong closing: **"I would tune the TTL per content type, long for versioned assets, short for HTML."**

notes: Trade-offs: freshness vs latency, edges vs hit rate and cost, shield vs extra hop

steps.model: A CDN trades **freshness and simplicity** for **latency and origin protection**: content can be stale until its TTL expires or it is purged, and there are more moving parts (routing, purge, cache layers). More edges mean lower latency but a lower hit rate per edge and higher cost. A shield layer lowers origin load but adds one more hop on a miss.
points: More edges: lower latency but lower hit rate per edge, higher cost
Shield cache reduces origin load but adds a hop on a miss
Operational complexity of the control plane
